questions.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),
$$

and ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0$

III. The curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$

*Hint: It is not necessary to use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the limit in part II.*
questions.worked_solution:
When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot 0} \\  & =\frac{-2}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the limit in part II does *not* equal to $0,$ there curve does *not* have a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$ In fact, it is a vertical tangent.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249911/assets/f4609e6433a861ef255cbeeac60c8a316e5c14a89df45030e26e526e3a1253a4.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-3\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{+},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\cancel{cos}\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{-}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{+}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249911/assets/50637a502a56fc242ba5d8e2fda59ddc899295d4b14f7ae692869536b95ef661.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Consider the polar curve $r={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=2\theta {cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-{\theta }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{\theta }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),
$$

and ${x}^{′}(0)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(0)=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =0$
questions.worked_solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}

$$

$$

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(0)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =0$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{0}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {0}^{-}$ using L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{\theta }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2\theta {cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-{\theta }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}{\theta (2{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{\cancel{\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}{\cancel{\theta }(2{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(0)-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)} \\  & =\frac{0}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
